record.original_question: How can model selection for biological systems be made statistically principled and computationally tractable when alternative models may have different effective parameter subspaces, many models can be nearly indistinguishable on available data, and the space of plausible models may not have any clear finite upper bound?

evidence.quote: Specifying the prior probability of models is notoriously difficult: in principle there is no clear a priori bound on the number of models, which could be (and arguably ought to be) infinite. This is a fundamental problem of, and a recurring theme in, Bayesian model selection.
The results of such an analysis can often be sobering, with many alternative model structures being virtually indistinguishable.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{M} = \{M_i\}_{i \in I}$ be a (possibly countably infinite) collection of candidate probabilistic models for a biological system. Each model $M_i$ specifies a parameter space $\Theta_i$ (which may have different dimensions and structure for different $i$) and a likelihood $p(D \mid \theta_i, M_i)$ for observed data $D$, together with a prior $\pi_i(\theta_i)$ on $\Theta_i$. A Bayesian model-selection procedure assigns prior probabilities $\{P(M_i)\}_{i \in I}$ with $\sum_i P(M_i) = 1$ and produces posterior probabilities
$$P(M_i \mid D) \;=\; \frac{P(M_i)\, \int_{\Theta_i} p(D\mid \theta_i, M_i)\, \pi_i(\theta_i)\, d\theta_i}{\sum_{j\in I} P(M_j)\, \int_{\Theta_j} p(D\mid \theta_j, M_j)\, \pi_j(\theta_j)\, d\theta_j}.$$
Three obstacles arise simultaneously:
(i) the index set $I$ has no natural finite upper bound and may need to be taken infinite;
(ii) different models may have effective parameter subspaces of differing dimensions, so that marginal likelihoods involve integrals over spaces that are not directly comparable;
(iii) on the data $D$ actually available, many models in $\mathcal{M}$ may yield nearly identical likelihoods, making them practically indistinguishable.

Devise a model-selection framework — specifying the choice of model prior $\{P(M_i)\}$, the within-model priors $\pi_i$, and an algorithm for computing or approximating the posterior $P(M_i\mid D)$ — that is (a) statistically principled (consistent and calibrated under reasonable assumptions on the data-generating process, and invariant under natural reparametrizations of $\Theta_i$), (b) computationally tractable for realistic biological data sets, and (c) robust to near-indistinguishability of models, in the sense that it explicitly quantifies and reports the resulting uncertainty rather than collapsing it onto a single model. Prove guarantees (e.g.\ consistency, contraction rates, or risk bounds) for the proposed framework.
artifact.status_search_result: Bayesian model selection over potentially infinite model spaces with non-nested parameter subspaces and near-indistinguishable alternatives is a longstanding foundational problem in Bayesian statistics. No general principled and computationally tractable solution is known; existing techniques (RJMCMC, nonparametric Bayes, ABC model choice, stacking, Bayesian model averaging) address parts of the problem but each has known limitations. The problem remains open as posed.
